Hip Injury in an Adult

fracture vs posterior dislocation by leg position · the 6-hour and 72-hour clocks · the shoulder mirror · reduction within about 6 hoursIs the leg externally rotated and abducted, or internally rotated, adducted and flexed?

1Presentation2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Older adult after a fall, groin pain, often cannot walk, leg may be shortened, abducted and externally rotated hip fracture: radiograph, then surgery once medically stable, within 72 hours
  • After a dashboard injury, leg shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated posterior dislocation: closed reduction as soon as possible, preferably within 6 hours
  • A normal radiograph with a fracture still suspected is not the end: MRI
What it is

An injured hip in an adult: a fracture of the femoral neck or between the trochanters, or a dislocation of the femoral head

Sort by

The leg position: shortened and turned out is a fracture; shortened, flexed and turned in is a posterior dislocation; flexed, abducted and turned out is the rare anterior one

Hands off

A fragility fracture: Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment; hip pain without injury: Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness; a child: The Limping Child

2Urgent risks
Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (avascular necrosis)After a displaced femoral neck fracture or a dislocation

If the hip is dislocated, choose closed reduction as soon as possible, preferably within 6 hours; open reduction if there is a fracture. Blood supplyThe femoral head depends on the medial circumflex femoral artery: a displaced neck fracture often disrupts it, and a dislocation left unreduced threatens the same tenuous supply.

Sciatic nerve injuryAfter a posterior dislocation

If a posterior dislocation, choose check sciatic nerve function, because the dislocation can injure it.

Venous thromboembolismImmobility after hip fracture surgery

If a hip fracture is repaired, choose prophylactic anticoagulation after surgery.

3Differential
Hip injury in an adult, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Femoral neck fractureOlder and osteopenic, a ground-level fall; leg shortened, abducted, externally rotatedRadiograph; displaced in an older patient: arthroplasty Femoral neck fractureA displaced femoral neck fracture in an older patient usually takes arthroplasty, so weight-bearing starts early; one who walks little usually gets a hemiarthroplasty. A nondisplaced or impacted fracture typically takes open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), and a younger patient may have early ORIF, within 6 hours. Intertrochanteric fractures usually take ORIF with an intramedullary nail or a dynamic hip screw.
Intertrochanteric fractureOlder, ground-level fall; leg shortened, abducted, externally rotatedFracture between the trochanters on radiograph; ORIF
Posterior hip dislocationThe most common dislocation; dashboard injury; leg shortened, flexed, adducted, internally rotatedReduce as soon as possible, preferably within 6 hours; CT after reduction for acetabular and femoral head fractures and loose bodies (an acetabular fracture in about 70% of these dislocations)
Anterior hip dislocationRare; leg flexed, abducted, externally rotatedReduce as soon as possible, preferably within 6 hours; the femoral head may be impacted or the cartilage injured
Impacted femoral neck fractureWalks with mild pain and no deformityRadiograph may be normal: MRI
Pubic ramus fractureGroin pain after a fallRadiograph
Osteonecrosis without injury (avascular necrosis)Long-term glucocorticoids or sickle cell disease; pain with weight bearing, no warmth or feverWeeks of progressive groin pain; radiograph often normal: MRI
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Knee pain after a fall in an older adultHip fracture with referred painHip radiographs
Displaced femoral neck fracture, 78 years oldFixation risks osteonecrosisArthroplasty
Dislocation reduced at 10 hoursHigher osteonecrosis riskWatch the femoral head
Fracture from a fall from standingOsteoporosisTreat the bone too
Shoulder after a seizure or electrocution, arm held turned inPosterior shoulder dislocation, the mirror of the hipAxillary and lateral radiographs

The shoulder mirrors the hip: the common anterior shoulder dislocation is held turned out (axillary nerve at risk), the rare posterior one turned in.

Pause point
Shortened leg after a dashboard injury Offered as a fracture Turned in and adducted → A dislocation; the 6-hour window is closing
Practice
  1. 78 yo F after a fall, leg shortened and externally rotated → Femoral neck fracture → X-ray, then arthroplasty
  2. 28 yo M after a head-on collision, leg shortened, internally rotated, adducted and flexed → Posterior hip dislocation → reduction within 6 hours
  3. 28 yo M with foot drop after a posterior hip dislocation → Sciatic nerve injury
  4. 78 yo F with a displaced femoral neck fracture → Arthroplasty → retinacular vessel disruption risks avascular necrosis (AVN)
  5. 28 yo M whose hip dislocation was reduced at 10 hours → Increased risk of femoral head osteonecrosis
  6. 70 yo M after a fall, leg shortened and externally rotated but abducted, groin pain → Intertrochanteric fracture
Time-critical Posterior dislocation needs reduction within ~6 hours to avoid femoral head AVN (avascular necrosis). In an older patient, a displaced femoral neck fracture carries osteonecrosis risk from retinacular vessel disruption; treat it with arthroplasty.
